Here are the verse-by-verse notes for Song of Solomon 3, drawn from the sources I could access.

---

## Song of Solomon 3 — Verse-by-Verse Notes

### Overview of the Chapter

Commentators broadly divide the chapter into two sections: **vv. 1–5**, the maiden’s dream (or the church’s seeking of Christ, in allegorical readings), and **vv. 6–11**, the wedding procession. Precept Austin, following Charles Swindoll’s chart, marks the chapter division at 3:5 as the end of “The Courtship” (Song 1:2–3:5) and the start of “The Wedding” (Song 3:6–5:1).¹

---

### v. 1 — *“On my bed at night I sought the one I love; I sought him, but did not find him.”*

- **It is probably a dream.** Guzik notes that this “snapshot probably records another dream or daydream of the maiden, as in the previous chapter,” since the section ends with her addressing the daughters of Jerusalem — unlikely to be physically present at a bedroom scene.² Constable agrees: “The Shulammite narrated an experience she had had ‘on her bed,’ namely, a dream.”³ The Preacher’s Outline and Sermon Bible (cited by Precept Austin) likewise calls it a “troubling dream” expressing fear of losing her beloved as marriage approached.⁴

- **The word “bed” carries sexual overtones.** Guzik cites Carr: “This is the common word for bed, distinct from the word for ‘couch’ in Song 1:16. In Ezekiel 23:17 the connotation is ‘love bed’… This is its only use in the Song.”⁵ Guzik adds that this reminds us of Hebrews 13:4 — the Bible celebrates sexual love within marriage but condemns it outside.⁶

- **Allegorical reading (Gill).** Gill interprets the “night” as a time of spiritual darkness, affliction, or desertion. “By night on my bed” represents a state of “carnal ease and security” in which the church sought Christ half-heartedly and therefore did not find Him. The Hebrew is plural (“by nights”), expressing that this went on night after night.⁷ The Catholic Haydock commentary similarly says Christ “had delayed coming at the usual hour, to give us to understand that he is not found amid delights.”⁸

- **Love deepens both joy and pain.** Guzik quotes Morgan: “Love creates a perpetual dread lest the loved one should be lost,” and Glickman: “Love not only brings a greater experience of joy, but a deeper capacity for pain as well.”⁹

- **The maiden’s healthy neediness.** Guzik observes: “The maiden allowed herself to feel needy without feeling helpless… she did not have an artificial sense of self-sufficiency.”¹⁰

- Spurgeon adds: “With what constancy she sought this communion. She began at dead of night, as indeed it is never too late to seek renewed fellowship.”¹¹

---

### v. 2 — *“I will arise now and go about the city, through the streets and squares. I will seek the one I love. So I sought him but did not find him.”*

- **Urgent, determined seeking.** Guzik highlights the immediacy (“I will arise now”) and her willingness to search everywhere — “in the streets and in the squares.” Her love drove her to act.¹²

- **Allegorical reading (Gill).** Perceiving that her previous method (staying on her bed of ease) had failed, the church now resolves to “rise” and seek Christ in “the public ordinances of the Gospel.” Even so, “I sought him, but I found him not” — to chasten her former negligence and to show that even the right means are not to be depended on apart from Christ’s sovereign will.¹³ Gill also notes the danger of a woman walking the city at night, showing the intensity of her love.¹⁴

- **The maiden’s pursuit follows an established relationship.** Guzik cautions: “There is something good in the maiden’s seeking of her beloved; yet it came after their relationship was well established. The relationship did not begin nor was it founded upon her pursuit of him.”¹⁵

---

### v. 3 — *“I encountered the watchmen on their rounds of the city: ‘Have you seen the one I love?’”*

- **The watchmen could not help.** Guzik notes that even though she was safe under their supervision, they could not point her to her beloved. He quotes Trapp: “It is probable that, lighting upon these watchmen, she promised herself much counsel and comfort from them, but was disappointed. It pleaseth God many times to cross our likeliest projects.”¹⁶

- **Allegorical reading (Gill).** The watchmen are “the ministers of the Gospel,” called watchmen in allusion to city watchmen and also to the prophets (Isaiah 52:8). They “go about the city” with diligence. When the church asks them, “Saw ye him whom my soul loveth?”, no answer is recorded — perhaps because she did not wait for one, or because she could not apply it to her case. Yet “she met with something from them that was of use to her afterwards.”¹⁷

- **Fourfold repetition.** Both Guzik and Precept Austin note that “the one I love” / “him whom my soul loves” appears four times in vv. 1–4, emphasizing her intense devotion.¹⁸

---

### v. 4 — *“I had just passed them when I found the one I love. I held him and would not let go until I had brought him to my mother’s house, to the chamber of the one who conceived me.”*

- **Diligent search rewarded.** Guzik: “She dreamt that her diligent search was rewarded. Though the watchmen… could not help her, she nevertheless found the one she loved.”¹⁹

- **“I held him and would not let him go.”** Guzik likens this to Mary Magdalene’s embrace of the risen Jesus (John 20:16–17).²⁰ Applying it devotionally, Spurgeon preached that “Jesus will go away if he is not held… He will go unless you hold him,” yet “Jesus is willing to be held” and “can be held” by faith.²¹

- **“Mother’s house” = marital, not illicit.** Several commentators stress this. Poole: “That there I might entertain and embrace him, and gain my mother’s consent, and so proceed to the consummation of the marriage.”²² Kinlaw: “She is not looking for an illicit consummation of their love. Consummation she wants, but even in her dream she wants the consummation to be right.”²³ Constable: “Her strong love for her beloved comes through… She dreams of consummation, but she wants the consummation to be proper.”²⁴ Kinlaw also notes the possible parallel with Isaac bringing Rebekah into Sarah’s tent (Genesis 24:67).²⁵

- **Allegorical reading (Gill).** “My mother’s house” may represent: (1) the visible church and its ordinances, the mother of all believers; (2) the heart and its inmost recesses where Christ dwells by faith; or (3) the heavenly mansions, “the Jerusalem above, the mother of us all.” The church resolves to hold Christ “till then… in the arms of faith, hope, and love.”²⁶

---

### v. 5 — *“O daughters of Jerusalem, I adjure you by the gazelles and does of the field: Do not arouse or awaken love until the time is right.”*

- **The refrain repeated.** This is the same charge found in Song 2:7. Guzik notes it confirms the dream setting: “We are not to imagine the couple together in the intimacy described in the previous lines with the daughters of Jerusalem observing.”²⁷

- **Meaning of the charge.** Guzik gives two dimensions: in terms of *relationship*, “Let our love progress and grow until it is matured and fruitful — don’t let us go too fast.” In terms of *passion*, “Let our love making continue without interruption until we are both fulfilled. Don’t let us start until we can go all the way.”²⁸ Constable: “Here the refrain marks the end of the section on the courtship… Solomon and the Shulammite’s patience were about to receive the desired reward. Their marriage was now at hand.”²⁹

- **Allegorical reading (Gill).** These may be Christ’s words to young converts not to disturb the church now resting with Him, or the church’s own words, “fearing these young converts should by any unbecoming word or action provoke him to depart.”³⁰

- **Catholic reading (Haydock).** The charge is understood within the allegorical drama; the church has found Christ and now warns others not to disturb this communion.³¹

---

### v. 6 — *“Who is this coming up from the wilderness like a column of smoke, scented with myrrh and frankincense from all the spices of the merchant?”*

- **The feminine “this” points to the bride, not Solomon.** Guzik highlights the Hebrew grammar: “The ancient Hebrew word translated *this* is in the feminine singular; the question ‘Who is this?’ is properly answered, ‘It is the maiden arriving in Solomon’s palanquin.’”³² Kinlaw concurs: “It is obviously a wedding procession… our picture is of the groom and his men bringing his bride from her home to his city for the wedding.”³³ The other occurrences of “Who is this?” in the Song (6:10; 8:5) also point to the maiden.³⁴

- **Barnes takes a different view** — that the citizens of Jerusalem or companions of the bridegroom “describe the magnificent appearance of the bride borne in a royal litter, and then that of the king in festive joy.”³⁵ The Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary says the feminine form “indicates the occupant is a woman,” but vv. 9–10 then describe Solomon’s separate conveyance.³⁶

- **“Coming up from the wilderness.”** Poole notes: “From whence we little expected to see so beautiful and glorious bride to come, such persons being usually bred in courts or noble cities.”³⁷ Clarke adds that “Going to Egypt was called descending or going down, coming from it was termed coming up.”³⁸

- **“Like pillars of smoke, perfumed.”** Carr (cited by Guzik) notes the Hebrew word for this smoke is used about 115 times with the meaning “make (a sacrifice) go up in smoke” — suggesting the smell of myrrh and frankincense comes from burning them as an offering.³⁹ Barnes describes the scene: “Frankincense and other perfumes are burned in such abundance round the bridal equipage that the whole procession appears from the distance to be one of moving wreaths and columns of smoke.”⁴⁰

- **Allegorical reading (Gill).** The daughters of Jerusalem, seeing the church now reunited with Christ, admire her. “The wilderness” represents either the state of nature before conversion, the world with its tribulations, or a state of spiritual desertion. The church comes out “like pillars of smoke” — her heart inflamed with love, her affections moving heavenwards.⁴¹

- **Catholic reading.** The Catholic Encyclopedia treats 3:6–5:1 as “clearly a description of the wedding-day,” where the two chief personages approach in stately procession.⁴² Haydock applies it to the church coming out of persecution.⁴³

---

### vv. 7–8 — *“Behold, it is Solomon’s carriage, escorted by sixty of the mightiest men of Israel. All are skilled with the sword, experienced in warfare. Each has his sword at his side prepared for the terror of the night.”*

- **Sixty groomsmen / bodyguards.** Guzik: “We might say that Solomon’s wedding party had sixty groomsmen. They weren’t there to keep Solomon from backing out of the wedding; they were there to show that he was a powerful man who could genuinely protect his maiden.”⁴⁴ Constable likewise calls them “very likely members of Solomon’s bodyguard,” noting his example of protection is one “every new husband should follow.”⁴⁵

- **“Terror of the night.”** Spurgeon, in his sermon on vv. 6–11, notes the historical danger: “When travelling through a wilderness, a royal procession was always in danger of attack. Arabs prowled around; wandering Bedouins were always prepared to fall upon the caravan; and more especially was this the case with a marriage procession.”⁴⁶ Barnes simply glosses it as “against night alarms” (cf. Psalm 91:5).⁴⁷

- **The shared life.** Guzik, quoting Watchman Nee: “She and Solomon were so identified with each other at this state that there was a perfect oneness between them. What was his, was hers. What he enjoyed, she enjoyed. This is union.”⁴⁸

- **Allegorical reading (Gill).** The “bed” or litter is the visible church; the sixty valiant men are ministers of the Gospel, faithful Israelites, holding the sword of the Word (Ephesians 6:17), expert in spiritual war, ready “because of fear in the night” — nights of desertion, temptation, affliction, and persecution.⁴⁹ Spurgeon likewise allegorizes the guards as defenders of the church: “There are enough guards for the church… valiant guards… well-armed, well-trained, always ready, and watchful.”⁵⁰

- **The Geneva Study Bible** (Reformed) reads the bed as “Solomon’s” — typifying Christ — with the mighty men representing the guard of God’s protection around His people.⁵¹

---

### vv. 9–10 — *“King Solomon has made his carriage out of the timber of Lebanon. He has made its posts of silver, its base of gold, its seat of purple fabric. Its interior is inlaid with love by the daughters of Jerusalem.”*

- **The palanquin’s opulence.** Guzik: “The maiden was impressed not only with the opulence of this palanquin, but especially that he shared all these symbols of authority and prestige with her.”⁵² He then draws the application: before marriage a man must be able to *protect* (the armed men) and *provide* (the opulent entourage) for his bride.⁵³

- **“Its interior inlaid with love.”** Barnes renders this as “its interior is paved with (mosaic work, or tapestry of) love from the daughters of Jerusalem” — meaning “this part of the adornment is a gift of love, whereby the female chorus have testified their goodwill to the bride.”⁵⁴ The NRSV Catholic Edition footnotes this phrase: “Meaning of Heb uncertain.”⁵⁵

- **Allegorical reading (Gill).** The “chariot” (or palanquin) represents the Gospel and its ministry: Christ made it “for himself,” it is of incorruptible cedar (“wood of Lebanon”), its silver pillars and gold base signify the preciousness and purity of Gospel truths, its purple seat signifies royalty, and the interior “paved with love” shows that love is the sum and substance of the Gospel.⁵⁶ Gill also notes the word translated “chariot” is used in the Mishnah for the nuptial bed or open chariot in which the bride was carried.⁵⁷

- **The Catholic Encyclopedia** identifies this section as belonging to the wedding-day portion of the Song, where “the bridal wreath and the bridal bed are referred to, and six times… the word spouse is used.”⁵⁸

---

### v. 11 — *“Come out, O daughters of Zion, and gaze at King Solomon, wearing the crown his mother bestowed on the day of his wedding — the day of his heart’s rejoicing.”*

- **Not the royal coronation crown.** Guzik, citing Carr, says this crown is “not the royal crown used in the coronation/consecration ceremony, but a ‘diadem’ or ‘wreath’ made either of branches (like the laurel wreath of the Olympic games), or of precious metals and stones.”⁵⁹ This connects to rabbinic tradition that a bride and bridegroom were considered a “royal couple” on their wedding day.⁶⁰

- **Why Bathsheba?** Guzik notes that the high priest, not Bathsheba, presided at Solomon’s royal coronation (1 Kings 1:38–40). So “his mother crowned him” likely refers to a wedding-day crowning — possibly hinting that the Song originated “in a time of relative innocence when Solomon was captivated by and attached to only one woman,” before his heart was drawn away to many women.⁶¹ Constable also notes this was “a special one his mother Bathsheba gave him for this occasion.”⁶²

- **The Abishag theory.** Guzik notes that some ancient and modern interpreters have associated the Shulamite (Song 6:13) with Abishag the Shunammite (1 Kings 1:3–4), but he cites Wiseman: “Shunem… lay eleven kilometers south-east of Nazareth… There is no need to identify Abishag with the Shulammite.”⁶³

- **“Daughters of Zion” vs. “daughters of Jerusalem.”** Barnes notes the distinction: “Daughters of Zion — So called here to distinguish them from the bride’s companions, who are always addressed by her as ‘daughters of Jerusalem.’”⁶⁴

- **Allegorical reading (Gill).** The daughters of Zion are invited to behold King Messiah. The crown His mother gave Him refers either to His human nature (which He received from His mother Mary according to the flesh) or to the crown His mother, the church (the heavenly Jerusalem), placed upon Him on the day of His espousals — His incarnation, passion, or the conversion of souls.⁶⁵

- **Catholic reading (Haydock).** “All are invited to come to Christ, who, in his sacred humanity, which he took of his mother, was crowned in heaven, after his passion.” It also notes that “the synagogue crowned him with thorns, and gave him the hard bed of the cross” (St. Bernard, St. Anselm).⁶⁶ Bathsheba “might live to see the marriage of her son, who owed the crown to her” (1 Kings 1:18; Proverbs 4:3).⁶⁷

- **Spurgeon** preached this as a call to behold Christ: “Go forth, O ye daughters of Zion, and behold King Solomon” — urging believers to contemplate Christ in His glory, crowned on the day of His heart’s gladness.⁶⁸

---

## Where Protestant Traditions Differ

### Allegorical vs. Literal Interpretation

This is the central divide running through Song of Solomon 3.

- **Reformed / Presbyterian.** Barnes (Presbyterian, 1832) reads the Song as principally about Solomon’s actual marriage, but acknowledges the Jewish and Christian allegorical traditions — e.g., “the ‘first’ entrance of the Church of the Old Testament into the land of promise” and “the espousals of the Church with Christ in the Passion and Resurrection.”⁶⁹ The Geneva Study Bible (Reformed) treats Solomon typologically as Christ.⁷⁰

- **Baptist.** Gill (Particular Baptist, 1746) is thoroughly allegorical: every detail points to Christ and the church. The bed is the visible church, the watchmen are ministers, the palanquin is the Gospel.⁷¹ Spurgeon (Baptist) likewise preaches the chapter allegorically — the maiden’s seeking is the believer seeking Christ, the sixty valiant men are guards of the church.⁷² Yet the Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary (1984) takes a more literal approach, calling vv. 1–5 “a dream sequence of the Shulamite” and vv. 6–11 “a royal procession.”⁷³

- **Methodist / Wesleyan.** Adam Clarke (Methodist, 1810) follows a more literal, historical reading. On v. 6 he says: “The bride, having risen, goes after her spouse to the country, and the clouds of incense arising from her palanquin seemed like pillars of smoke.”⁷⁴ Wesley’s Notes (available on StudyLight) are brief but similarly literal in tendency.⁷⁵

- **Pentecostal / Charismatic.** David Guzik (Enduring Word, Calvary Chapel) takes the Song as primarily about human love and marriage, read literally, but with typological application to Christ and the church drawn secondarily. He states clearly: “In either interpreting or applying Song of Solomon 3:1–4 to the relationship between Jesus and His people, many commentators have noted that this is an example of how the believer… must seek after Him.”⁷⁶ He also cites Watchman Nee (a major figure in the Chinese house-church movement) for the “union” application.⁷⁷

- **Lutheran.** No detailed Lutheran commentary on this chapter was retrieved from the specified sites (lcms.org, 1517.org). The StudyLight aggregator lists only 1–2 Lutheran commentators on v. 6, but their specific content was not available in the excerpts.⁷⁸

---

## Other Views

### Modern Scholarship (NET Bible / bibleodyssey.org)

The NET Bible notes for Song 3 were referenced by Precept Austin but the full notes could not be fetched. However, Precept Austin’s page for Song 3 indicates the NET notes are “synchronized with Thomas Constable’s notes,”⁷⁹ and Constable takes a literal, historical-grammatical approach: the Song is about human love and marriage, with the wedding procession in 3:6–11 being a historical description of ancient Israelite wedding customs.⁸⁰

### Catholic and Orthodox Readings

- **Catholic.** The Catholic Encyclopedia states that the Song’s “actual meaning” is not limited to any one application: it applies to the Church, to the most holy Humanity of Jesus, to the Blessed Virgin Mary as “the most beautiful flower of the Church,” and to the individual purified soul.⁸¹ Haydock’s commentary (used in the Douay-Rheims tradition) reads the chapter allegorically: vv. 1–5 describe how “the Church, finding Christ by his own revelation, and not by philosophy, holds him fast,” and vv. 6–11 describe Christ crowned in heaven after His passion.⁸²

- **Orthodox.** No material from oca.org on this specific chapter was retrieved.

### The “Shepherd Hypothesis” (Three-Character Drama)

James Burton Coffman (Church of Christ, 1971) champions the view that there are *two* male lovers in the Song — Solomon and the Shulamite’s shepherd sweetheart. In his reading, vv. 6–11 are *not* a wedding procession for the Shulamite but “Solomon’s grand parade to the northern residence of the Shulamite with the purpose of bringing her back to Jerusalem.” He argues that the absence of any mention of a bride in the procession and the implausibility of Solomon being a type of Christ make the traditional reading untenable. He goes so far as to call Solomon “an effective type of the devil himself” in this passage.⁸³ Coffman’s view is a minority position among commentators but represents one clearly documented alternative.
